skill: Sample Statistics and Margin of Error

stimulusShape.structure: A research-report paragraph stating (a) who was sampled and how ('a random sample of 200 city residents'), (b) a sample statistic (a percentage like 52%, or a mean like 42 grams with units), and (c) an associated margin of error ('with an associated margin of error of 3%'). Variants report two candidates/groups each with estimate and margin, or state a sample-size change and ask about its effect. Every quantity needed appears in the passage; no figure or table is used.

stemTemplates: Based on the survey, which of the following is a plausible value for the percent of all <population> who <behavior>?
Which of the following statements is supported by the survey results?
What effect does increasing the sample size have on the margin of error?
Which of the following best describes why the margin of error is needed in this survey?
choicePatterns: Four STATEMENTS (not numbers), each a full claim about the estimate, the interval, the population, or the effect of sample size — exactly one consistent with the reported statistics. A statement distractor is a named misconception expressed as a study claim: the point estimate declared exact, the interval taken one-sided, a larger sample declared more uncertain, or a biased sample declared representative. Plausible-value variants embed numbers inside the statements (a value outside estimate ± ME).

distractorLogic.trap: Statement distractor claiming the margin of error increases (or is unchanged) when the sample size grows: 'The margin of error would increase to more than 3%' for a repeat with 400 residents. Expresses the no-directional-model bug as a design claim about n.

Statement or value distractor applying the margin to the wrong quantity or one side only: offers 55% (estimate + ME only) as the interval's upper end phrased as 'between 52% and 55%', or a plausible value just outside 49-55% rejected/accepted with the band shifted. Built by mutating exactly one side or one unit of the correct interval claim.

Statement distractor extending the result to a population the sampling frame does not cover: 'The survey shows that about 52% of all city residents exercise weekly' when only gym members were surveyed. Expresses the representativeness bug as a generalization claim.

Statement distractor asserting certainty: 'The percent of all residents who exercise weekly is exactly 52%' or ruling out 54% as impossible. Expresses the point-estimate bug as a precision claim; built by deleting the interval qualifier from the true claim.

easy: Single random sample, one percentage with margin; plausible-value choices where one sits inside the interval and three sit far outside (by 5+ points)
Direction-of-effect item with a large sample-size doubling (100 to 10,000) so 'decreases' is discriminable
Interval endpoints are whole numbers and the interval is wide
medium: Plausible-value choices hovering just at and just beyond the interval endpoints (e.g., key 54, distractors 55, 48, 56 for 52 ± 3)
Two groups with overlapping intervals asked whether a difference is established ('Group A 48 ± 4 vs Group B 54 ± 4: can it be concluded A < B?')
Why-margin-of-error items mixing correct-precision claims with exact-value claims
hard: Sample-size effect asked quantitatively ('ME roughly like 1/sqrt(n): 100 -> 400 cuts ME from 6% to about 3%')
Biased-frame items where the numbers are perfect but the sample source is off (gym members for city residents)
Nested claims: each choice combines a plausible value AND a generalization scope, and only one matches both the interval and the sampled population
Reconciling two surveys with different sample sizes and non-overlapping vs overlapping intervals

generationRecipe.stimulusConstruction: 1. Choose a population and behavior (city residents, voters, a school's students; weekly exercise, approval of a policy, owning a bike). 2. Pick n from 50-500 (typically 100-400) and a percentage from 15-85 so the interval stays inside 0-100. 3. Set ME to 2-6 percentage points, wider for smaller n. 4. State the sampling method — random for most items, deliberately biased (a subpopulation or voluntary poll) for the representativeness items. 5. Close with the report sentence citing estimate and margin verbatim.
generationRecipe.keyConstruction: Interval: estimate - ME to estimate + ME; plausible values are those strictly inside (endpoint inclusion stated in the stem when used). Effect of n: ME shrinks as n grows (roughly 1/sqrt(n) — doubling n fourfold roughly halves ME). Valid generalization scope: exactly the population that was randomly sampled. Verify the interval endpoints stay within [0, 100] and that the key claim names only quantities or scopes the passage supplies.
generationRecipe.distractorConstruction: STATEMENT-DISTRUCTOR PATTERN (this archetype does not compute numeric keys for its choices): each wrong choice is a named misconception rendered as a study-design claim, in the same sentence shape as the key so surface reading cannot discriminate. Templates: (a) 'The margin of error would increase/stay the same' for a sample-size change; (b) 'between <estimate> and <estimate + ME>' / plausible values one point outside the true band; (c) '<estimate>% of ALL <wider population> ...' for a biased frame; (d) 'exactly <estimate>%' / 'a value of <inside-band> is not plausible'. Write each by mutating exactly ONE element of the true claim (a side, a scope, a hedge word, a direction), then confirm only the key survives re-reading the passage's numbers and sampling description.
validationChecklist: Survey totals 50-500; percentages 15-85; margins of error 2-6 whole points; interval stays within 0-100
Every choice is a complete sentence in the key's grammatical shape — numbers appear inside statements, not as naked options
Exactly one choice is consistent with the passage's estimate, margin, sample size, and sampling frame
Each distractor mutates exactly one element of the true claim and maps to a single misconception id
Plausible-value items state endpoint handling ('between 49% and 55%, inclusive' or values strictly between) so the key is unambiguous
The passage states WHO was sampled; generalization-scope choices match or overreach that stated population precisely

answerComputation: Plausible values: estimate - ME <= v <= estimate + ME (52% ± 3% gives the band 49-55%). Sample-size effect: ME decreases as n increases (roughly 1/sqrt(n); quadrupling n roughly halves ME). Valid claims: point estimates are not exact — only interval-level statements are licensed. Verify by recomputing the band and re-checking the sampling frame named in the passage.
numericConstraints: n from 50-500 (typical 100-400); percentages 15-85 (whole numbers); margins of error 2-6 whole percentage points; interval endpoints whole numbers within 0-100; no numeric grid-in answers (choices are statements).
questionTypeNotes: Nearly all mcq — this archetype's answers are STATEMENTS, so it contributes no grid_in items. The generator must build four claim sentences per item, not four numbers: replicate the key's sentence shape and mutate one element per distractor (direction of ME change, one interval side, generalization scope, hedge word). Reading-level similarity across choices is deliberate and required.
